digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-08
digests.theme: Today is a mechanism-or-it-is-just-a-waveform day. The strongest clinical-translational paper is Suppression of pathological oscillations with transcranial focused ultrasound in Parkinson’s disease, because it finally asks focused ultrasound to do something tougher than produce an fMRI blob or a vague behavioral effect: push a disease-linked electrophysiological biomarker in the therapeutically correct direction. The strongest computational paper is Adversarial AI reveals mechanisms and treatments for disorders of consciousness, which matters less as an AI branding object than as a serious attempt to force a large discriminative system and an interpretable neural-field model to constrain each other. The most useful methods-side paper is Transcranial focused ultrasound induces source localizable cortical activation in resting state humans when applied concurrently with transcranial electric stimulation, mainly because it is willing to say the awkward part out loud: in resting humans, ultrasound alone mostly looked like auditory or deep-brain confound structure, while localized cortical responses emerged only when paired with concurrent electrical stimulation.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Suppression of pathological oscillations with transcranial focused ultrasound in Parkinson’s disease. This is a very small proof-of-concept study, so nobody should talk as if ultrasound is ready to replace deep brain stimulation. But the paper is still important because it uses implanted subthalamic recordings in Parkinson patients to test a much cleaner claim than the usual noninvasive-neuromodulation rhetoric. Four male participants in a randomized controlled cross-over design received pallidal transcranial ultrasound pulsed at 130 hertz. The authors report a roughly 10.3 percent reduction in ipsilateral subthalamic beta power and a 17.7 percent reduction in bradykinesia indexed by reaction time, with correlated beta suppression between the ipsilateral subthalamic nucleus and motor cortex. The sample is tiny and the confidence bounds are correspondingly fragile, but this is still one of the more legible recent ultrasound papers because it targets a known disease biomarker rather than decorative whole-brain activation.

The second paper is Adversarial AI reveals mechanisms and treatments for disorders of consciousness. What makes it worth attention is not that it uses AI. Plenty of papers use AI and become more boring as soon as they say so. The interesting move here is the adversarial coupling between a high-capacity classifier trained on more than 680,000 ten-second neuroelectrophysiology samples and interpretable neural-field models intended to generate realistic conscious and comatose dynamics. The authors claim the framework recovers specific mechanistic signatures associated with unconscious states, including selective disruption of the basal ganglia indirect pathway and increased cortical inhibitory-to-inhibitory coupling, and then nominate subthalamic stimulation as a treatment candidate for disorders of consciousness. That is unusually ambitious. It also means the burden of proof is high. Still, as a computational-control paper, it is more useful than average because it tries to connect representation learning, mechanistic simulation, and intervention logic rather than stopping at classification accuracy.

The third keep-worthy paper is Transcranial focused ultrasound induces source localizable cortical activation in resting state humans when applied concurrently with transcranial electric stimulation. This is a methods and platform paper, not a clinical result, and it may actually be more valuable for that reason. The core finding is that focused ultrasound by itself did not yield convincing target-localized cortical activation in these resting-state EEG experiments, whereas combined transcranial electro-acoustic stimulation, or tEAS, did. The paper also shows that several ultrasound-only responses were statistically consistent with auditory pathway activation and deep-brain projections rather than the intended cortical target. That makes this paper a useful brake on ultrasound hype. It also suggests a more interesting engineering direction: use ultrasound as a spatially precise subthreshold modulator that needs another excitability context, rather than pretending it is already a standalone noninvasive deep-stimulation replacement.

A fourth paper stayed below note threshold but remains citation material: Deep Brain Stimulation Response Circuits in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. It is a synthesis review, not a new primary study, but it is useful as a compact summary of where connectomic OCD-DBS and adaptive biomarker work are converging.
digests.takeaway: The pattern today is that neuromodulation looks strongest when papers stop hiding behind generic modulation language and instead make explicit claims about mechanism, state, and controllable circuit variables. The Parkinson ultrasound study matters because it targets a biomarker that already has real therapeutic meaning. The disorders-of-consciousness AI paper matters because it tries to force machine learning into contact with interpretable dynamics and intervention hypotheses. The tEAS paper matters because it shows that ultrasound-only stories in humans may still be confound-heavy, and that hybrid stimulation may be a more honest route to localized control. Put together, the lesson is simple: if a modality cannot show what state variable it changes, in what direction, and why that variable matters, the field should trust it less.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-07
digests.theme: Today is a network honesty over target folklore day. The strongest paper is Parkinson's disease as a somato-cognitive action network disorder, because it is unusually willing to say that Parkinson intervention logic should be framed around a distributed action-and-body-control network rather than around isolated motor effectors or inherited target tribalism. The most directly useful neuromodulation mechanism paper is Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans, which gives actual longitudinal, individual-level circuit readouts under multiple DBS stimulation regimes instead of pretending symptom change alone is enough. The computational anchor is Competitive interactions shape mammalian brain network dynamics and computation, which is not a stimulation study, but it matters because it challenges the cooperative-only assumptions that quietly sit underneath a lot of network-control and connectome-targeting stories.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Parkinson's disease as a somato-cognitive action network disorder. This is not just another Parkinson connectomics paper. The authors assemble a large multimodal, multi-intervention dataset and argue that the key dysfunction is hyperconnectivity between subcortical Parkinson circuitry and the somato-cognitive action network, or SCAN, rather than a problem localized to classical effector-specific motor territories. That claim matters for neuromodulation because the paper does not stop at descriptive connectivity. It links successful interventions across deep brain stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation, MRI-guided focused ultrasound, and levodopa to reduction of SCAN-to-subcortex hyperconnectivity. The most provocative practical finding is that TMS targeted to functionally defined SCAN cortex reportedly outperformed effector-region targeting by about twofold in their study. That is the kind of result that can easily be overhyped, but even discounted, the paper is directionally important because it turns target selection into an explicit network hypothesis.

The second paper is Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans. This is the cleaner mechanism paper for actual DBS. Fourteen Parkinson patients with MRI-compatible subthalamic nucleus implants were scanned before surgery and then four times over the following year under seven stimulation conditions, including off stimulation, high-frequency, low-frequency, and variable-frequency settings. The key contribution is not merely that stimulation changes the brain. The paper estimates individualized functional parcellations and connectomes, then shows that DBS engages separable pallidal and motor-cortical circuits with different temporal and frequency profiles. High-frequency stimulation performed best clinically on average. More importantly for future work, the study is a template for how neuromodulation should be studied when the goal is personalization rather than marketing.

The third keep-worthy paper is Competitive interactions shape mammalian brain network dynamics and computation. It belongs here because network-guided neuromodulation keeps borrowing from whole-brain models and control language that assume long-range coupling is effectively cooperative unless proven otherwise. This paper relaxes that assumption and shows across human, macaque, and mouse data that whole-brain models allowing competitive interactions fit empirical dynamics better, produce more realistic metastability and hierarchy, and are more subject-specific. That does not immediately tell you where to stimulate a patient tomorrow. But it does pressure-test a lot of simplistic network-control intuition. If the best generative account of macroscale dynamics already includes long-range competition, then intervention logic built on purely cooperative propagation may be structurally naive.

A fourth paper stayed below note threshold but remains worth remembering: Dose-response relationships in transcranial brain stimulation: Physics, physiology and mechanism. It is a review rather than a new mechanism result, so it did not earn a preserve note today. Still, it is a useful reminder that dose in TMS, transcranial electrical stimulation, ultrasound, and electroconvulsive therapy is not a single scalar knob, and that cross-modality comparisons often hide mismatched physical and physiological definitions.
digests.takeaway: The pattern today is that neuromodulation gets more interesting when the field stops pretending its network priors are already settled. The SCAN paper is the most important because it links disease framing, target selection, and treatment response across several intervention classes. The precision neuroimaging DBS paper is the strongest direct methods contribution because it measures individualized circuit responses with enough temporal and longitudinal depth to matter. The competitive-interactions modeling paper is the conceptual guardrail, because it argues that whole-brain dynamics are shaped not just by cooperation but by long-range competition as well. Put together, the day points toward a stricter standard for network-guided intervention: specify the circuit, specify the state logic, and make sure the model underneath the targeting story is not fake-simple.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-06
digests.theme: Today is a signal honesty before personalization theater day. The strongest new paper is the PMC preprint Predicting monopolar local field potential power from bipolar recordings in deep brain stimulation, because it attacks a boring but central problem that a lot of adaptive-DBS rhetoric skips past: the implant usually senses in bipolar space, while biomarker and programming claims are often made as if contact-specific monopolar information were directly available. The most interesting clinical paper is Untangling neurophysiology of Tourette syndrome using dual-target bi-pallidal deep brain stimulation, which is tiny but at least tries to separate anterior-versus-posterior pallidal logic instead of flattening GPi into a single magical target. The computational anchor remains the recent arXiv paper Passivity-Based Control of Electrographic Seizures in a Neural Mass Model of Epilepsy, which is not new to the repo but still matters because it forces closed-loop seizure-control claims to say what structural properties of the system actually justify the controller.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Predicting monopolar local field potential power from bipolar recordings in deep brain stimulation. The reason is simple: a lot of so-called precision neuromodulation quietly rests on a measurement mismatch. Chronic devices prefer bipolar recordings because they are cleaner, but the field still wants to reason about contact-specific physiology as if it had monopolar access for free. This paper reframes that mismatch as a stable inverse problem. Using intraoperative recordings from sixty-four Parkinson patients with subthalamic or pallidal implants, the authors use selected bipolar montages and robust linear regression to estimate monopolar band power. The reported performance is strong enough to take seriously, with adjusted R-squared values near zero point nine. That does not prove better outcomes, but it directly sharpens the representational layer underneath adaptive programming.

The second keep-worthy paper is Untangling neurophysiology of Tourette syndrome using dual-target bi-pallidal deep brain stimulation. This is a three-patient pilot, so nobody should pretend it settles target selection. What makes it worth preserving is the framing. The authors implant both anterior and posterior GPi regions, record postoperative local field potentials, and ask whether those subregions may map differently onto tic reduction and psychiatric symptom changes. The signal is small but suggestive: the two patients with the clearest tic reduction showed prominent posterior-GPi high-beta activity, while acute cross-modulatory effects between anterior and posterior GPi were not consistent. The value is less the headline efficacy and more the move toward symptom-component and circuit-subregion thinking.

The third paper worth attention today is Passivity-Based Control of Electrographic Seizures in a Neural Mass Model of Epilepsy. It is not a new note today, but it belongs in the digest because it complements the other two papers at the control-logic level. The paper argues that seizure dynamics in the standard Epileptor setting are neither passive nor naturally passivatable, yet sufficiently strong passive feedback can still stabilize them and output redesign can make passivity arguments viable. That matters because a lot of closed-loop seizure-control language jumps directly from simulation to controller righteousness. This paper makes the assumptions legible.

A fourth paper that stayed adjacent but below preserve threshold is The mechanism of external cueing interventions in improving freezing of gait in Parkinson’s disease: an fNIRS study. It is not neuromodulation in the stimulation-device sense, but it is still relevant to state-transition framing. The useful part is that single auditory or visual cues improved gait and increased cortical activation in prefrontal and somatosensory regions, while combined cueing did not simply stack benefits. I kept it below note threshold because the mechanistic interpretation is still thin and the intervention is cueing, not stimulation.
digests.takeaway: The pattern today is that intervention claims get stronger when the representation and control layers are made explicit. The monopolar-reconstruction paper is the best of the set because it improves the measurement logic that many adaptive DBS ideas quietly rely on. The Tourette dual-target paper is underpowered but directionally good because it treats one named target as an internal circuit problem rather than a single coordinate. The passivity-control epilepsy paper remains important because it insists that control language should cash out in system properties, not just in simulation success. Overall, this was a good day for infrastructure and logic, not for grand efficacy claims.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-05
digests.theme: Today is a personalization claims under stress day. The strongest paper is the Brain study Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study, because it uses multi-year implanted recordings to ask a question the field keeps dodging: can we see response trajectories early enough to guide therapy rather than waiting passively for slow clinical drift. The most translationally provocative paper is the Research Square preprint Pre-ictal signature-guided individualized closed-loop tTIS suppresses seizures onset in pediatric epilepsy, which is ambitious and clinically attractive but currently too abstract-level and too preprint-dependent to trust without caution. The most interesting computational paper is the arXiv preprint Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model, which is strong on scale and framing but still lives in the danger zone where personalized virtual brains can become high-gloss response prediction theater.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study. The valuable part is not that it found yet another biomarker. The valuable part is that it used four years of longitudinal anterior thalamic recordings from twenty-two patients to examine whether response to anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation leaves a durable physiological trace rather than only a delayed clinical one. According to the abstract, responders progressively shift toward higher-frequency anterior thalamic activity and away from lower-frequency activity, and simple high-to-low spectral ratios can discriminate eventual clinical outcome early. That does not prove a ready-made adaptive controller, but it is the right level of question: can the implant tell you whether therapy is converging or stalling before you waste months.

The second keep-worthy paper is Pre-ictal signature-guided individualized closed-loop tTIS suppresses seizures onset in pediatric epilepsy. This is exactly the sort of paper that needs both attention and skepticism. The appealing claim is clear: a deep-learning framework integrates thirty-three EEG features in forty-five pediatric patients to derive a personalized pre-ictal threshold, then uses that threshold to trigger transcranial temporal interference stimulation in thirteen patients and six macaques. The paper says the personalized interventions suppressed seizure onset. If that holds up, it is a serious advance in proactive seizure control. But almost everything important is still unresolved from accessible text alone: exact detector calibration, false-alarm burden, stimulation geometry, comparison against simpler baselines, and what "suppressed" means operationally.

The third preserve-worthy paper is Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model. This is a big claim paper, but it is not obviously empty. The authors pretrain a generative virtual-brain model on a large resting-state fMRI collection, then finetune on Parkinson cohorts receiving temporal interference or deep brain stimulation and use counterfactual healthy-versus-pathological state estimates to predict treatment response. The headline metrics are strong, including external and prospective validation in small additional cohorts. The reason to keep it is not that virtual-brain foundation models are automatically trustworthy. The reason is that it reframes outcome prediction around patient-specific state transition modeling rather than only static biomarkers. Still, this could collapse into sophisticated overfitting if the individualized generative machinery is less identifiable than the paper suggests.

A fourth paper that stayed in scope but below the preserve threshold is Phase estimation with autoregressive padding, or PEAP: addressing inaccuracies and biases in EEG analysis. It may end up mattering more than some flashier intervention studies because real-time phase-targeted stimulation is only as good as the phase estimator. The paper reports that common methods are systematically biased and that PEAP improves accuracy while reducing edge artifacts. That is useful and probably real. I kept it just below the note threshold today because the immediate translational consequence is methodological hygiene rather than a direct intervention result.
digests.takeaway: Today’s pattern is that personalization only matters if the control logic survives contact with time, noise, and heterogeneity. The best paper is the anterior thalamic DBS study because it deals with slow therapeutic drift and asks whether implanted physiology can reveal response trajectories early. The pediatric tTIS paper is ambitious and worth preserving precisely because it could be important, but right now it reads like a high-upside claim in need of a much harsher methods audit. The virtual-brain Parkinson paper is the right kind of computational ambition — state modeling instead of decorative prediction — but it is still at serious risk of becoming elegant overfitting if the model’s mechanistic interpretation outruns its evidence.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-04
digests.theme: Today is a control logic versus hardware theater day. The strongest preserve-worthy paper is the bioRxiv preprint Passive neuromodulation: an energy-driven mechanism for closed-loop suppression of epileptic seizures, because it states a clean intervention idea instead of treating stimulation as magic: if seizure dynamics can be damped by draining energy from the circuit, then responsive control may not need to look like conventional pulse-train stimulation at all. The most interesting translational hardware paper is Remote Magnetomechanical Neuromodulation Uncovers Therapeutic Mechanisms for Alleviating Parkinsonian Symptoms in Freely Moving Mice, which is flashy but not empty. The most useful targeting and network infrastructure paper is A human subcortical connectome at 400 μm resolution, because serious neuromodulation still lives or dies on whether the field can resolve the subcortical pathways it keeps pretending to target.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Passive neuromodulation: an energy-driven mechanism for closed-loop suppression of epileptic seizures. This is not a clinical paper and it does not pretend to be. Its claim is narrower and more interesting: using two seizure models, the authors argue that an analog feedback element can passively drain energy from an epileptic circuit and suppress seizure initiation or spread without the usual active stimulation logic. They report efficacy in both a detailed dentate-gyrus network model and the Epileptor neural mass model, and they also test a responsive version that turns on for brief windows after seizure detection. The reason to keep this is not that it is ready for patients. The reason is that it sharpens a neglected control idea: some pathological dynamics may be better handled by damping than by repeated forcing. That is a better mechanistic frame than a lot of decorative closed-loop rhetoric.

The second paper worth preserving is Remote Magnetomechanical Neuromodulation Uncovers Therapeutic Mechanisms for Alleviating Parkinsonian Symptoms in Freely Moving Mice. This one has obvious hardware-hype risk, but it is more substantial than the phrase minimally-invasive DBS without chronically implanted hardware would suggest. The core design uses magnetite nanodiscs that generate local torque under low-frequency alternating magnetic fields, aiming to recruit endogenous mechanosensory pathways rather than electrodes or optogenetics. The paper reports in vitro and ex vivo calcium-imaging evidence, remote control of motor behavior in wild-type mice, and improved motor function in a severe hemiparkinsonian mouse model when targeting the subthalamic nucleus. That is interesting translational engineering, but it is still preclinical, and the jump from mechanosensory torque in mice to clinically meaningful human deep-brain control remains enormous.

The third preserve-worthy paper is A human subcortical connectome at 400 μm resolution. This is not a stimulation study, but it may matter more than many nominal stimulation papers because it targets a real bottleneck: the subcortical pathways behind deep brain stimulation and lesion effects are hard to resolve with ordinary diffusion MRI, so the field leans on synthetic or overly smoothed atlases. This paper uses ultra-high-resolution ex vivo diffusion MRI on the Connectome 2.0 scanner to reconstruct basal-ganglia-thalamocortical pathways and then align the resulting atlas to reported deep brain stimulation hotspots and side-effect zones. It should not be mistaken for patient-ready individualized targeting, but it is exactly the kind of anatomical infrastructure that can make future targeting claims less hand-wavy.

A fourth paper that stayed in scope but below the preservation threshold is Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG. It is useful methods work. The strongest part is that it avoids prediction-heavy phase targeting and instead directly detects phase in real time, improving trigger probability and phase precision for event-related theta in navigation tasks. But the accessible evidence here is validation without active TMS delivery, so for now it is better treated as a promising platform paper than as a direct intervention result.
digests.takeaway: Today’s honest pattern is that the strongest ideas were not the loudest hardware claims. The best paper is the seizure-control preprint because it makes the intervention logic more explicit: some pathological brain dynamics may be better damped than driven. The magnetomechanical Parkinson paper is worth keeping because it is a real preclinical modality paper, not pure branding, but it still lives far from human therapeutic proof. The subcortical connectome paper is valuable because targeting cannot improve if the anatomy stays blurry. And the phase-targeting TMS paper is a good reminder that better timing infrastructure is useful, but not every precision method deserves immediate preserve status as an intervention result.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-03
digests.theme: Today is a deep-target-engagement versus control-ambition day. The strongest new paper is a Nature Communications study using individualized transcranial ultrasound stimulation to hit the human globus pallidus internus and read out local field potentials through implanted deep brain stimulation leads. That is rare direct evidence of deep-target engagement from a nominally noninvasive modality. The strongest clinical context paper remains the randomized PTSD trial using individualized functional MRI guidance for transcranial magnetic stimulation, because it continues to set a better-than-usual bar for circuit-based psychiatric targeting. On the computational and network side, I scouted broadly, but most of the newest titles were still stronger as framing material than as preserve-worthy notes.
digests.overview:
The most relevant new paper today is Individualized non-invasive deep brain stimulation of the basal ganglia using transcranial ultrasound stimulation. The useful part is not the phrase non-invasive DBS, which is marketing-dangerous on its face. The useful part is narrower and better: the authors used subject-specific acoustic simulations, targeted the globus pallidus internus in patients who already had implanted DBS systems, and then recorded local field potentials from that deep target while delivering ultrasound. Theta-burst ultrasound increased theta power during stimulation, ten-hertz ultrasound increased beta power, and some effects lasted up to forty minutes. In healthy participants, globus pallidus internus stimulation also worsened stop-signal performance while pulvinar stimulation did not, which at least argues for some target specificity. This does not prove ultrasound is ready to replace implanted DBS. It does show direct human deep-target engagement with physiological and behavioral consequences, which is a materially stronger claim than most ultrasound neuromodulation papers can support.

The second paper worth attention is Personalized fMRI-Guided TMS Targeting the Threat Neurocircuitry in PTSD: A Randomized Clinical Trial. It is not new to the repo anymore, but it remains one of the better recent examples of a psychiatric neuromodulation study trying to make target logic, mechanistic endpoint, and later symptom outcome live in the same trial. Active stimulation reduced right amygdala threat reactivity relative to sham, while delayed symptom outcomes favored active treatment. Skin conductance did not move, and the immediate symptom separation was not clean, so this is not a triumphal precision-psychiatry story. But it is still a more serious targeting paper than most.

The third item is Multimodal branched transport infers anatomically aligned brain reaction maps. This is adjacent inspiration rather than a preserve-worthy note. The idea is to infer routed propagation architectures from multimodal data instead of assuming a fixed network and only optimizing transition cost. That is conceptually aligned with intervention logic, because routing matters for where stimulation effects spread. But at abstract level this still looks more like a mathematical framing paper than a demonstrated neuroscience tool. Interesting, yes. Ready to preserve as a practical note, not yet.

A fourth title that surfaced repeatedly was Counterfactual Analysis of Brain Network Dynamics. I am explicitly not preserving it today. The framing sounds appealing, but at accessible depth it still reads like intervention language wrapped around a Hodge-theoretic decomposition without enough empirical burden-bearing. That may mature into a useful citation later, but today it looks more like theory packaging than something that changes how we would build or evaluate a neuromodulation system.
digests.takeaway: The useful lesson today is that direct target engagement matters more than grand control vocabulary. The ultrasound globus-pallidus paper is worth keeping because it actually measures a deep target while perturbing it and shows some behavioral specificity. The PTSD TMS paper remains useful because it ties target choice to a symptom-relevant circuit instead of generic scalp heuristics. By contrast, several fresh computational-network titles sounded intervention-relevant but still carried more mathematical ambition than empirical burden. So today’s honest pattern is simple: preserve the paper that proves it touched something real, keep the serious circuit-targeting clinical trial as context, and do not let elegant theory language crowd out stronger mechanistic evidence.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-02
digests.theme: Today is a targeting-and-dynamics day. The strongest clinical paper is a randomized PTSD trial using individualized functional MRI guidance to pick a transcranial magnetic stimulation target connected to the right amygdala. The strongest computational paper is JEDI: Jointly Embedded Inference of Neural Dynamics, not because it is immediately intervention-ready, but because it tries to infer shared and condition-specific dynamical structure across tasks instead of fitting one recurrent network per silo. The strongest network-level translational paper remains the pediatric vagus nerve stimulation study on intrinsic network resilience and interictal perturbation, but that note already existed in the repo, so it functions here as confirmation rather than as a new preserve-worthy addition.
digests.overview:
The most relevant new paper today is Personalized fMRI-Guided TMS Targeting the Threat Neurocircuitry in PTSD: A Randomized Clinical Trial. The useful part is not the phrase personalized. The useful part is that the personalization logic is actually tied to a circuit hypothesis: find the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex site with the strongest functional connection to the right amygdala, then test whether low-frequency stimulation changes amygdala threat reactivity and symptoms. The result is not clean triumph. The mechanistic endpoint moved, the immediate autonomic endpoint did not, and the clearest symptom separation appears at follow-up rather than right after treatment. But this is still a better-formulated targeting paper than most psychiatric TMS work.

The second new paper worth preserving is Jointly Embedded Inference of Neural Dynamics. It is adjacent rather than clinical, but it matters because it attacks a real bottleneck in mechanistic modeling: most data-constrained recurrent models are trained condition by condition, which makes cross-task comparison awkward and generalization weak. JEDI proposes a hierarchical embedding over recurrent weights so that condition-specific dynamics live in a shared space. If that framework holds up beyond the abstract, it could be useful for state-transition framing, subject-condition comparison, and eventually for control-oriented modeling.

The third paper worth calling out is Time-Varying Directed Interactions in Functional Brain Networks: Modeling and Validation. This is more methods than intervention, but it is a respectable methods paper because it tries to estimate time-varying directed interactions rather than recycling sliding-window correlation. The multimodal validation, task sensitivity, and clinical application to post-concussion vestibular dysfunction make it more credible than a purely synthetic benchmark paper. Still, it is a directed-connectivity method paper, not a direct neuromodulation result, so it belongs in the useful-but-adjacent bucket.

A fourth paper remains important context rather than a new note: Association of Brain Network Perturbations With Response to Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Children With Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy. It already has a note in the repo, but it still deserves mention because it reinforces the same theme as the PTSD paper and JEDI paper: treatment heterogeneity and intervention logic become more legible when you model networks as dynamic and perturbable rather than as static correlation maps.
digests.takeaway: The useful papers today all refuse static thinking. The PTSD trial treats TMS targeting as a circuit-selection problem tied to amygdala reactivity. JEDI treats neural dynamics as something that should be modeled jointly across tasks and contexts rather than separately memorized. The directed-connectivity paper treats brain networks as time-varying and directional rather than as undirected similarity blobs. Even the already-preserved pediatric VNS paper fits the same pattern: response depends on network resilience to perturbation, not just on baseline labels. So the broader lesson is simple. Better neuromodulation work is moving toward explicit state, circuit, and perturbation logic. The field is still far from clean control theory in humans, but at least the better papers are asking questions in that direction.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-01
digests.theme: Today is a model-versus-evidence day. The strongest conceptual paper is a generative virtual-brain preprint for predicting Parkinson's neuromodulation response from resting-state functional MRI, because it at least tries to connect individualized network models to counterfactual treatment estimation instead of throwing another opaque classifier at a tiny cohort. The most practically grounded translational paper is a Parkinson's decoding study that compares noninvasive electroencephalography and invasive electrocorticography for motor-state decoding under deep brain stimulation on and off conditions. The most clinically provocative paper is a long-term post-traumatic stress disorder deep brain stimulation follow-up, but it is only four patients, so the signal is interesting and the overclaim is not.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model. If the abstract survives fuller scrutiny, it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to use individualized network modeling for treatment selection rather than mere post hoc biomarker reporting. The attractive part is not the phrase foundation model. The attractive part is the counterfactual logic: pretrain a large generative model of resting-state brain dynamics, adapt it to each patient, then estimate how far stimulation moves that patient toward a healthier state and whether that movement predicts outcome. That is at least the right shape of question.

The second paper worth keeping is Invasive and Non-Invasive Neural Decoding of Motor Performance in Parkinson's Disease for Personalized Deep Brain Stimulation. It is smaller and less glamorous, but it is more honest than many adaptive deep brain stimulation papers because it shows what can and cannot be decoded in a mixed invasive and noninvasive setup, and it explicitly ties the decoding story to behavior under stimulation rather than treating biomarkers as detached trophies.

The third paper is Long-term outcome of subgenual cingulum and uncinate fasciculus deep brain stimulation for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder. This is clinically intriguing because durable improvement in severe post-traumatic stress disorder would matter a lot, and the tract-level target choice is at least mechanistically legible. But the cohort is four patients. So this is a keep-for-context paper, not a settle-the-field paper.
digests.takeaway: The useful papers today share one virtue: they make the intervention logic more explicit. The virtual-brain paper says treatment response should be predicted by how stimulation moves an individualized network model, not just by static biomarkers. The Parkinson's decoding paper says adaptive control needs behavior-linked, patient-specific signals measured under real stimulation conditions, not generic frequency-band mythology. The post-traumatic stress disorder deep brain stimulation follow-up says tract-aware psychiatric targeting may be worth continuing, but it still lives in feasibility-land. So today is less about triumphant evidence than about better-formulated control and targeting questions.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-31
digests.theme: Today is a targeting-logic versus evidence-depth day. The strongest clinical paper is a randomized head-to-head transcranial magnetic stimulation trial in major depression showing that two connectome-derived targets can differentially shift anxiety versus depressive symptom burden. The strongest network paper is a pediatric vagus nerve stimulation study arguing that baseline anterior network integrity and resilience to interictal perturbation help explain who responds. The strongest computational paper is a control-theory preprint that finally tries to put rigorous passivity analysis under seizure suppression rather than merely simulating another closed-loop heuristic. Together they point at the same practical lesson: personalized neuromodulation gets more credible when targetable circuits, state perturbations, and controller assumptions are made explicit rather than hidden inside syndrome labels.
digests.overview:
The most decision-relevant paper today is Circuit-targeted modulation of anxiety symptoms in individuals with major depression: A randomized head-to-head TMS trial because it prospectively tests a symptom-specific connectomic targeting claim instead of selling it retrospectively. The result is useful but not magical: both targets improved depression similarly, while the dorsomedial anxiosomatic target improved anxiety more strongly. That is a real step toward symptom-selective intervention logic, though the sample is still small and the trial is not a full personalization study.

The most mechanistically useful paper is Association of Brain Network Perturbations With Response to Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Children With Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy. It does not give a deployable predictor yet, but it is better than generic biomarker fishing because it links response to both baseline alpha-band network organization and post-IED microstate resilience. That makes the heterogeneity story more circuit-legible.

The most conceptually useful paper is Passivity-Based Control of Electrographic Seizures in a Neural Mass Model of Epilepsy. It is still model-land rather than clinic-land, but it does something rare and valuable: it asks whether seizure dynamics in a standard neural mass model are even compatible with a passivity-based feedback design, and what sensor and output redesign choices are mathematically required if they are not.
digests.takeaway: The best work today is trying to earn the word precision by specifying what varies across patients and what exactly a controller or target is supposed to do. The TMS trial suggests symptom-specific circuit targeting may have prospective value, but only modestly and in a small sample. The VNS network paper makes response heterogeneity more intelligible by tying it to anterior network organization and perturbation resilience rather than demographics or seizure topography. The control-theory paper is further from practice, yet useful because it tightens the formal language around seizure suppression. So the field looks strongest when it replaces broad syndromic neuromodulation claims with explicit circuit, perturbation, and control assumptions.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-30
digests.theme: Today is a control-logic versus clinical-proof day. The strongest clinical hit is a randomized phase 3 anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation trial in drug-resistant epilepsy after vagus nerve stimulation failure, but it lands in the awkward zone between clinically meaningful effect sizes and statistically non-superior between-group proof. The strongest computational hit is an arXiv paper arguing that brain stimulation should be framed as stochastic trajectory tracking rather than one-shot state steering. The most useful mechanistic support paper is a beta-oscillation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation study showing that timing relative to beta phase matters more than generic stimulation delivery. Together they sharpen the same point: neuromodulation gets more legible when the control objective is explicit, but most of the field still validates the objective weakly.
digests.overview:
The most decision-relevant paper today is Deep brain stimulation of the thalamus for intractable epilepsy (FRANCE study): A randomized clinical trial because it is an actual phase 3 comparison in a hard population that had already failed vagus nerve stimulation. It is clinically important, but it does not cleanly prove superiority over best medical treatment; the between-group p-value misses conventional significance despite a numerically better seizure reduction and responder rate.

The most conceptually useful paper is A new perspective on brain stimulation interventions: Optimal stochastic tracking control of brain network dynamics. It is not treatment evidence, but it is one of the cleaner recent arguments that intervention goals should be framed as synchronizing unhealthy dynamics toward healthy dynamics, not merely forcing one state vector to another at a single time point.

The best mechanistic adjunct is Characterising motor and cognitive contributions of cortical beta oscillations and their modulation with rTMS. It is a healthy-participant study, so no one should over-translate it, but it gives a more explicit account of what beta-frequency stimulation may be doing: lowering a movement-initiation threshold, with stronger effects when timed to the beta down state.
digests.takeaway: The clean lesson today is that better control language is arriving faster than better proof. The epilepsy trial gives real translational signal, but not definitive superiority. The stochastic tracking paper gives a more realistic computational objective for intervention, but remains far from deployable clinical control. The beta-frequency rTMS paper clarifies one plausible mechanism knob, yet only in healthy volunteers. So the field is getting better at saying what it wants stimulation to do over time, but it still too rarely closes the loop from control objective to target engagement to robust patient benefit.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-29
digests.theme: Today is a programming-and-deployment logic day. The best hits are not grand theory papers; they are papers that make neuromodulation decisions more explicit: a multicenter sham-controlled portable HD-tACS trial in depression, a connectome-guided DBS programming paper for Parkinsonian gait dysfunction, and a mechanistic-but-still-clinical Parkinson’s DBS asymmetry paper showing target-dependent rebalancing effects. The useful pattern is that symptom- or state-specific control logic is getting sharper, while a lot of the field still remains thin on prospective validation.
digests.overview: The most decision-relevant paper today is A multicenter randomized clinical trial of portable transcranial alternating current stimulation for major depressive disorder because it is a real sham-controlled multicenter trial rather than the usual tiny stimulation teaser. The most mechanistically useful paper is Towards connectome-guided optimization of deep brain stimulation for gait dysfunction, which treats gait as a symptom-specific programming problem instead of assuming standard clinically optimized DBS settings should already be optimal for everything. Pallidal and subthalamic stimulations modulate inter-hemispheric interaction and asymmetry in Parkinson's disease is worth keeping as adjacent mechanistic support: it links target choice to baseline asymmetry direction and to changes in inter-hemispheric coupling, though it is more explanation than actionable control. I am demoting today’s earlier Tourette and naturalistic accelerated-TMS picks below these newer papers; they are still worth preserving, but they are not the sharpest items in today’s final cut.
digests.takeaway: The honest picture today is that neuromodulation gets more useful when the control problem is stated clearly. The portable HD-tACS depression trial matters because it finally tests a scalable noninvasive protocol in a real randomized multicenter design. The connectome-guided gait DBS paper matters because it acknowledges that one symptom may need a different programming objective than another. The Parkinson’s asymmetry paper is a smaller but still useful sign that target effects are not just about mean motor improvement; they can reshape lateralization and network coupling in baseline-dependent ways. The broader lesson is good: explicit optimization and symptom-specific logic are improving faster than our prospective validation standards.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-28
digests.theme: Today’s strongest pattern is that good neuromodulation papers are getting more explicit about circuit response and less convincing when they overpromise personalization. The best paper is a serious individual-level DBS neuroimaging study that actually tries to map what stimulation is doing over time and across frequencies. The most useful clinical paper is a negative rTMS trial in chronic pain showing that a plausible connectivity-based targeting idea did not beat standard M1 targeting. The most interesting hardware preprint is a deep-stimulation relay concept that is clever but still very early.
digests.overview: The most worth-preserving paper today is Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans because it goes after a question the field keeps hand-waving around: what circuits does DBS modulate in actual individuals, under different frequencies, over time? Personalizing neuromodulation for chronic pain: A connectivity-guided randomized trial is valuable precisely because it is a negative result: global connectivity-guided targeting did not improve outcomes, which is useful pressure against decorative “personalization” rhetoric. A minimally invasive floating-wire interface for transcranial deep brain stimulation is adjacent inspiration rather than near-term translational evidence; the idea is technically interesting, but the current evidence is simulations, benchtop validation, and rodent motor-threshold work.
digests.takeaway: The honest read today is that neuromodulation gets more interesting when papers expose circuit structure and less interesting when they sell targeting heuristics as personalization. The DBS precision-neuroimaging study is worth keeping because it combines deep longitudinal measurement with parameter variation and individual network estimation. The chronic-pain trial is worth keeping because it shows a reasonable connectivity-guided targeting idea can still fail clinically. FLOATES is worth remembering as a clever minimally invasive concept, but not yet as evidence that deep noninvasive-ish stimulation has solved its core translational problems.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-27
digests.theme: Today’s useful papers are mostly about infrastructure for control and mechanism, not near-term psychiatric efficacy. The strongest computational paper makes large, biologically constrained circuit fitting much more tractable. The strongest neurotechnology paper builds an implant platform that is materially closer to ecological, bidirectional neuromodulation than the usual tethered lab rig. The taVNS cognition papers, by contrast, mostly illustrate why weak behavioral enhancement claims without physiological verification remain hard to take seriously.
digests.overview: The most worth-preserving paper today is Deep-learning-assisted simulation of a cortical circuit: integrating anatomy, physiology and function because it pushes mechanistic large-scale circuit modeling out of the supercomputer-and-hand-tuning era into something more reproducible and attackable. A modular, high-bandwidth, bidirectional implantable device for neural interrogation is the strongest translational hardware hit: not because it proves a therapy, but because it provides a plausible route toward chronic, bidirectional, modular sensing-and-stimulation setups that could support real closed-loop work outside toy conditions. The recent taVNS electrical-vs-ultrasound cognition papers are lower-confidence and mostly negative-to-mixed; they are worth noting as a reminder that “noninvasive vagal enhancement” remains parameter-fragile and mechanism-light in healthy volunteers.
digests.takeaway: The strong pattern today is that the worthwhile papers improve the machinery of inference and intervention rather than claiming premature therapeutic victory. The cortical simulation paper improves our ability to fit and interrogate biologically constrained circuits. The MBI paper improves the hardware substrate for chronic bidirectional interfacing. The taVNS studies mostly show the opposite pattern: lots of intervention language, modest behavioral signal, and weak mechanistic verification. So the honest read is that infrastructure and modeling are advancing faster than many of the flashy human neuromodulation effect claims.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-26
digests.theme: The useful neuromodulation papers today are less about raw efficacy and more about whether the intervention logic is legible. The strongest work either (a) ties outcome prediction to an actually recorded circuit signal, (b) makes targeting variability explicit instead of pretending scalp heuristics are precise, or (c) shows a manipulable mechanism at the cell/circuit level. The weaker work still likes grand network stories assembled from normative connectomes and retrospective aggregation.
digests.overview: Today’s strongest hit is the BNST-NAc DBS depression paper because it combines a randomized clinical design with perioperative physiology, longitudinal tracking, and a biomarker story that is at least specific enough to attack. The precision TMS modeling paper is useful because it exposes how sloppy standard dlPFC targeting still is and gives a practical individual-network targeting workflow, though it remains a targeting/modeling paper rather than an outcome trial. The tFUS rat paper is adjacent rather than translational, but it is one of the cleaner recent mechanism papers because it links parameter regime to bidirectional circuit effects and identifies a specific cell-type contribution. A depression “common therapeutic network” paper is worth noting mainly as framing/citation material; it is ambitious and interesting, but much of the causal language outruns what secondary network mapping can really support.
digests.takeaway: The real pattern today is that the better papers are forcing neuromodulation to become more explicit about control variables. The BNST-DBS study says: here is the signal, here is how it predicts outcome, here is how it moves with stimulation. The TMS modeling paper says: here is why your supposed target is not reliably the same target across people. The tFUS paper says: here are the parameter regimes and neuronal populations behind opposite effects. That is the right direction. By contrast, the common-network depression paper is interesting synthesis but still too inferential to carry much mechanistic weight on its own.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-25
digests.theme: Personalized neuromodulation is slowly becoming more real: invasive mapping and adaptive control papers are starting to specify where, when, and why to stimulate instead of just reporting another average effect size. The good work is still narrow and early. The weak work still loves grandiose claims.

The Parkinson adaptive DBS trial matters because it moves aDBS from short in-clinic demos toward longer at-home use, though the endpoint framing is softer than one would like. The closed-loop tACS-fMRI paper is an interesting noninvasive proof of concept, but the sample is tiny and the behavioral gain is modest. The Parkinson aDBS trial shows that chronic sensing-driven stimulation is operationally viable at scale, but the control logic is still relatively simple and the endpoint framing is not pristine. notes.title: Transcranial focused ultrasound induces source localizable cortical activation in resting state humans when applied concurrently with transcranial electric stimulation
notes.whySelected: It is a useful anti-hype methods paper because it suggests that focused ultrasound alone may not produce clean target-localized cortical activation in resting humans, whereas a hybrid ultrasound-plus-electric setup can.
notes.verdictText: This is a methods paper with real value because it is willing to report the uncomfortable result. Ultrasound alone did not convincingly produce localized cortical activation in the reported resting-state EEG setup, while combined transcranial electro-acoustic stimulation did. That makes the paper more useful than many cleaner-sounding platform papers because it clarifies what may actually be required for controlled human cortical engagement.
notes.overview: The study compares focused ultrasound alone, transcranial direct current stimulation controls, and combined transcranial electro-acoustic stimulation, or tEAS, in resting-state humans using simultaneous whole-scalp EEG and source localization. The authors report that only the combined tEAS conditions produced significant hemisphere-specific and source-localizable cortical responses in the targeted region of interest, whereas tFUS alone mainly produced responses consistent with symmetric auditory or deep-brain activations. They also ran broader parameter searches and still found no convincing evidence that ultrasound alone yielded target-localized suprathreshold cortical stimulation. The practical implication is that ultrasound in humans may function better as a spatially precise subthreshold modulator that needs another excitability context rather than as a standalone direct cortical activator.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it prevents sloppy thinking about ultrasound. If the modality mostly acts as a context-dependent modulator rather than a clean standalone activator, that changes how targeting, control, and device design should be framed.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful methods note. Not a direct therapy paper, but a strong correction to lazy ultrasound narratives and a good clue about more realistic neuromodulation engineering directions.

notes.title: Suppression of pathological oscillations with transcranial focused ultrasound in Parkinson’s disease
notes.whySelected: It is one of the first recent human ultrasound papers that tries to move an established Parkinson circuit biomarker in the therapeutically correct direction rather than settling for vague activation claims.
notes.verdictText: This is a small but genuinely important proof-of-concept. The sample is tiny, so nobody should confuse it with a mature therapeutic result, but the paper asks a stricter question than most noninvasive neuromodulation studies: can pallidal ultrasound suppress subthalamic beta activity, a disease-linked biomarker already tied to Parkinson pathophysiology and adaptive stimulation logic? That makes it much more useful than another ultrasound paper that only reports a behavioral nudge or an fMRI blob.
notes.overview: The paper tests whether transcranial ultrasound stimulation can noninvasively modulate pathological oscillations in Parkinson’s disease in the same broad circuit direction as effective deep brain stimulation. In a randomized controlled cross-over design, four male Parkinson patients received pallidal ultrasound pulsed at 130 hertz while the investigators measured subthalamic local field activity and behavior. The headline claim is that ipsilateral STN beta-band power fell by about 10.34 percent, the reduction tracked suppression in ipsilateral motor cortex, and bradykinesia measured through reaction time improved by about 17.7 percent. The result is far too small to settle therapy, but it is conceptually strong because it uses an established biomarker target instead of generic “neuromodulation” language.
notes.whyItMatters: Because this is the kind of paper that makes noninvasive neuromodulation less embarrassing. It does not prove therapy, but it does force the modality to answer a serious question about circuit control rather than hiding behind generic claims about modulation.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. Small, fragile, and not yet clinically dispositive, but unusually worth preserving because the intervention logic is much cleaner than average.

notes.title: Adversarial AI reveals mechanisms and treatments for disorders of consciousness
notes.whySelected: It is a rare computational paper that tries to force large-scale classification, interpretable neural-field mechanism, and intervention hypothesis generation into the same pipeline for disorders of consciousness.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the more interesting recent AI-for-neuroscience papers because it does not stop at decoding conscious versus comatose states. The useful ambition is that it pits a high-capacity discriminative system against interpretable neural-field models so the model family has to generate dynamics that look biologically real and classification-relevant at the same time. The caveat is that papers like this can overstate the strength of the bridge from recovered mechanism to treatment recommendation, so the intervention claims should be read more as constrained hypotheses than as validated clinical guidance.
notes.overview: The paper introduces an adversarial AI framework for disorders of consciousness in which deep neural networks trained to detect consciousness from more than 680,000 ten-second neuroelectrophysiology samples are coupled to interpretable neural-field models that try to simulate conscious and comatose brain states. The authors report validation across 565 patients, healthy volunteers, and animals, and claim the framework recovers mechanistic features of unconscious states, including selective disruption of the basal ganglia indirect pathway and increased cortical inhibitory-to-inhibitory coupling. The stronger-than-usual move is that they do not treat those mechanisms as purely descriptive. They use the generative framework to nominate subthalamic nucleus stimulation as a treatment candidate for disorders of consciousness, with supporting alignment to diffusion MRI and RNA-sequencing evidence. That is ambitious enough to be worth preserving and risky enough to deserve skepticism.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is exactly the sort of paper that could sharpen how we think about state estimation and intervention logic if it survives scrutiny. Even if some of the treatment claims soften later, the framework itself is a serious attempt to connect decoding, dynamics, and control.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. Potentially very important for mechanistic control framing, but it should be carried with an explicit warning label: treatment relevance is still a hypothesis path, not a settled therapeutic result.

notes.title: Parkinson's disease as a somato-cognitive action network disorder
notes.whySelected: It makes an unusually explicit network-level claim about Parkinson's disease and then tries to connect that claim to response across DBS, TMS, MRI-guided focused ultrasound, and levodopa.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the more interesting recent intervention-framing papers in Parkinson's disease because it does not just say a network exists. It argues that a specific distributed system, the somato-cognitive action network or SCAN, is the relevant cortical partner for multiple subcortical Parkinson targets and that successful treatment reduces SCAN-to-subcortex hyperconnectivity. That is a bold claim and will need replication, but it is much more useful than another paper that treats target choice as folklore plus motor scores.
notes.overview: The paper asks whether Parkinson's disease is better understood as dysfunction of a distributed action-control network rather than of isolated effector-specific motor circuits. Using a large multimodal dataset spanning resting-state imaging, electrocorticography, DBS, transcranial magnetic stimulation, MRI-guided focused ultrasound, and levodopa response, the authors claim that classic Parkinson-relevant subcortical nodes are preferentially connected to the somato-cognitive action network rather than to effector motor cortex. They further report that patients show elevated SCAN-to-subcortex connectivity compared with controls, and that effective interventions reduce this hyperconnectivity. The most practically provocative result is that TMS aimed at functionally defined SCAN cortex reportedly performed substantially better than effector-region targeting.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is exactly the kind of paper that can sharpen intervention logic if it holds up. It says stop talking about targets like isolated coordinates and start asking which distributed action-control circuit you are actually perturbing.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a core reference for Parkinson network-targeting and intervention framing. Strong, useful, and worth skepticism in exactly the right places.

notes.title: Competitive interactions shape mammalian brain network dynamics and computation
notes.whySelected: It is a strong whole-brain modeling paper because it tests a hidden assumption inside a lot of network-control and connectome-guided intervention rhetoric: that long-range interactions should be modeled as cooperative by default.
notes.verdictText: This is not a neuromodulation outcome paper, but it is very relevant infrastructure for thinking about network interventions. If the best generative models of brain dynamics require long-range competitive as well as cooperative interactions, then simplistic intervention logic based on purely cooperative spread is probably missing something important.
notes.overview: The paper asks whether whole-brain models should allow competitive, effectively net-negative interactions between regions rather than assuming that long-range coupling is always cooperative. The authors build species-specific generative models for human, macaque, and mouse brains using structural connectivity plus functional MRI, compare cooperative-only against cooperative-plus-competitive architectures, and examine the resulting dynamics and computational properties. Across species, the models allowing competition fit empirical data better, were more subject-specific, and produced more realistic hierarchy, synergy, and metastability. The result is less a clinical prescription than a better dynamical prior for any attempt to think seriously about network control or stimulation.
notes.whyItMatters: Because a lot of network-targeted neuromodulation talk quietly assumes that if you perturb one node the rest of the system mainly cooperates along positive pathways. This paper says the underlying dynamical prior may be more antagonistic, more hierarchical, and more realistic than that.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a conceptual anchor for network-control, connectome-guided targeting, and mechanistic modeling. Not a therapy paper, but exactly the sort of adjacent infrastructure paper that improves future intervention thinking.

notes.title: Untangling neurophysiology of Tourette syndrome using dual-target bi-pallidal deep brain stimulation
notes.whySelected: It is a small but mechanistically relevant DBS paper that tries to relate anterior-versus-posterior GPi physiology to different Tourette symptom dimensions instead of treating pallidal targeting as a monolith.
notes.verdictText: The sample is tiny, so this is nowhere near target-settling evidence. But it is still worth keeping because it pairs dual-target pallidal implantation with postoperative local field potential recordings and symptom follow-up, which is exactly the sort of design that can start separating motor and non-motor effects instead of relying on target folklore. Treat it as an existence proof for richer target-disentangling studies, not as a practice-changing result.
notes.overview: This pilot study examines whether anterior and posterior globus pallidus internus targets in severe Tourette syndrome may carry distinguishable physiological and clinical roles. Three medication-refractory patients underwent dual-target bi-pallidal DBS, and the investigators recorded local field potentials under different stimulation conditions while also tracking tic severity, psychiatric symptoms, and quality of life over time. The headline signal finding is that high-beta activity in posterior GPi was prominent in the two patients with the clearest tic reduction, whereas acute cross-modulatory spectral effects between anterior and posterior GPi were not consistently observed. The useful read is that the paper nudges the field toward symptom-component and circuit-subregion logic, even though the evidence remains extremely preliminary.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a small but real example of intervention logic getting more granular. If psychiatric and movement symptoms recruit partly separable nodes, then personalized DBS should mean more than choosing one fashionable coordinate.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a small mechanistic pilot. It is too underpowered to anchor clinical claims, but it is exactly the sort of study that can sharpen future target logic for complex symptom mixtures.

notes.title: Predicting monopolar local field potential power from bipolar recordings in deep brain stimulation
notes.whySelected: It attacks a real adaptive-DBS bottleneck: chronic devices usually give you bipolar recordings, but programming and biomarker logic often want contact-specific monopolar estimates.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the more useful recent DBS methods papers because it solves an immediate representational problem instead of proposing another vague biomarker. The core claim is modest and practical: with a well-chosen set of bipolar montages, monopolar band-power estimates can be reconstructed accurately enough to improve spatial disambiguation for programming and adaptive stimulation. The limitation is that it is still a retrospective regression paper in Parkinson cohorts, not a clinical outcome study.
notes.overview: The paper asks whether contact-specific monopolar local field potential power can be inferred from the bipolar signals that implanted DBS hardware more naturally records. Using intraoperative recordings from sixty-four Parkinson patients implanted in subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus internus targets, the authors generate bipolar montages across contacts, compute power spectral density in canonical bands, and fit robust linear regression models that map selected bipolar powers to monopolar powers at each contact. The useful point is not machine-learning novelty. The useful point is that they turn a hardware-imposed measurement constraint into an estimation problem that may make chronic sensing more spatially interpretable without changing the implant.
notes.whyItMatters: Because a lot of adaptive-DBS rhetoric quietly assumes cleaner and more localizable signals than devices really provide. This paper matters by narrowing that gap in a practical way. It sharpens the representation layer underneath targeting, state estimation, and biomarker-guided control.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. It is a methods paper, not treatment evidence, but it directly improves the signal logic beneath adaptive DBS and is more useful than many flashier biomarker papers.

notes.title: Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model
notes.whySelected: It is worth preserving because it tries to predict neuromodulation response through individualized state modeling and counterfactual neural trajectories rather than through a plain black-box outcome classifier.
notes.verdictText: This is ambitious in a way I mostly approve of: it tries to make response prediction look like patient-specific dynamical modeling instead of decorative biomarker hunting. The upside is real, especially because the paper reports both deep brain stimulation and temporal interference cohorts plus external and prospective validation. The main problem is that abstract-level evidence is nowhere near enough to prove the generative virtual-brain story is identifiable, leakage-resistant, or mechanistically interpretable.
notes.overview: The paper proposes a pretraining-finetuning framework that learns a generative virtual-brain foundation model from a large resting-state fMRI collection and then adapts it to Parkinson cohorts undergoing neuromodulation. The authors say the pretrained model captures broad disorder patterns across more than two thousand subjects and over five thousand sessions, after which patient-specific finetuning yields individualized virtual brains for temporal interference and deep brain stimulation cohorts. They then estimate counterfactual transitions between pathological and healthy neural states inside these personalized models to predict clinical response. The core attraction is the framing: outcome prediction becomes a question about individualized state reconfiguration under stimulation rather than only a static classifier over connectivity features.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it pushes neuromodulation prediction toward explicit state-transition reasoning. Even if this particular model ends up partially theater, the direction is right: response prediction should be tied to a model of how stimulation reconfigures a diseased dynamical system.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as an adjacent computational reference with serious upside and serious overclaim risk. Worth tracking, not worth blindly trusting.

notes.title: Pre-ictal signature-guided individualized closed-loop tTIS suppresses seizures onset in pediatric epilepsy
notes.whySelected: It is a high-upside closed-loop neuromodulation paper because it moves from generic seizure detection toward personalized pre-ictal triggering for noninvasive intervention, even though the current evidence is still too thin to trust fully.
notes.verdictText: This could be important if the full methods hold up, because proactive seizure suppression using individualized pre-ictal signatures is exactly the kind of control logic the field needs. But right now the paper sits on a dangerous combination of strong claims and limited accessible detail. The abstract makes the project sound cleaner than most seizure-control papers, yet it leaves too many unanswered questions about baselines, detector reliability, stimulation dose, and actual clinical outcome definition.
notes.overview: The paper describes a personalized closed-loop framework for pediatric epilepsy that derives a pre-ictal electrophysiological signature from scalp EEG and uses that signature to trigger transcranial temporal interference stimulation before seizure onset. The authors say they integrate thirty-three EEG features from forty-five pediatric patients to define a dynamic pre-ictal personalized prediction threshold, or Pi-PPT, which can identify vulnerable states up to twenty minutes before seizure. They then deploy Pi-PPT-guided stimulation in thirteen epileptic patients and six macaques and report suppression of seizure onset. The attractive idea is obvious: move from reactive stimulation after seizure emergence to pre-emptive intervention timed to each patient’s own pre-ictal dynamics.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it embodies the right control ambition: detect a patient-specific impending state transition and intervene before the system falls into the bad basin. Even if this exact implementation turns out overclaimed, the framing is worth keeping.
notes.finalDecision: Keep, but with a loud warning label. The intervention logic is exactly the sort of thing worth following, while the current evidence remains preprint-level and too underspecified to trust without the full paper.

notes.title: Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study
notes.whySelected: It is one of the more useful recent epilepsy DBS papers because it asks whether implanted thalamic physiology can reveal therapeutic response trajectories before clinicians are forced to wait on slow noisy clinical outcomes.
notes.verdictText: This is not causal proof of an adaptive biomarker, but it is a serious translational paper because it works on the right timescale and with the right clinical nuisance. Anterior thalamic DBS effects in epilepsy are delayed, variable, and hard to monitor, so a multi-year observational dataset is more valuable than yet another short-term stimulation demo. The main caution is that abstract-level access leaves too many unresolved details about seizure-ground-truth quality, programming heterogeneity, and whether the spectral markers are robust or simply correlative drift.
notes.overview: The paper studies twenty-two patients with drug-refractory epilepsy who underwent anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation and contributed longitudinal intracranial recordings over four years. The authors look for neurophysiological signatures that distinguish responders from non-responders and that might predict or track treatment benefit earlier than clinical observation alone. According to the abstract, responders show a progressive shift toward higher-frequency anterior thalamic activity, especially beta-one and gamma, along with reduced delta and theta activity, and high-to-low frequency ratios such as beta-one over theta can separate future responders early. The practical point is not just biomarker discovery. It is whether the implant can provide a running measure of therapeutic convergence.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it treats epilepsy DBS like a slow feedback-control problem rather than a mystical implant therapy. The important idea is early trajectory sensing: if you can tell that therapy is moving in the right physiological direction, you can intervene sooner and program more rationally.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a core clinical-translational reference for biomarker-guided epilepsy DBS, with the explicit warning that it remains observational until prospective programming studies prove the markers are actionable.

notes.title: Remote Magnetomechanical Neuromodulation Uncovers Therapeutic Mechanisms for Alleviating Parkinsonian Symptoms in Freely Moving Mice
notes.whySelected: It is a nontrivial preclinical attempt to build an electrode-free deep-target neuromodulation modality with mechanistic and behavioral evidence.
notes.verdictText: This is more serious than gadget theater, but it is still preclinical and should be read with a tight leash on the hype. The paper is worth preserving because it links a novel actuator to mechanosensory pathways, deep-target delivery logic, and measurable behavior in a Parkinsonian mouse model. It is not remotely close to proving an outpatient substitute for human deep brain stimulation.
notes.overview: The paper introduces a remote magnetomechanical neuromodulation approach that uses magnetite nanodiscs exposed to low-frequency alternating magnetic fields to generate localized piconewton-scale torques. The claimed mechanism is that these torques activate endogenous mechanosensory pathways, enabling neuromodulation without chronically implanted electrodes or genetic modification. The authors report calcium-imaging evidence for rapid effects in vitro and ex vivo, then apply the method to the subthalamic nucleus in mice. They report remote modulation of motor behavior in wild-type animals and improved motor function in a severe hemiparkinsonian model. The translational promise is obvious, but the evidence remains at the preclinical proof-of-concept stage.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is the kind of modality paper that is worth tracking without falling in love with it. It broadens the intervention palette while forcing the question of what evidence a new actuator must show before it deserves translational attention.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful modality note. Interesting and nontrivial, but still very far from clinical neuromodulation reality.

notes.title: Passive neuromodulation: an energy-driven mechanism for closed-loop suppression of epileptic seizures
notes.whySelected: It is a computationally sharp reframing of seizure control as energy damping rather than conventional active stimulation.
notes.verdictText: This is not translational evidence and it should not be sold that way. But it is one of the better recent computational neuromodulation papers because it contributes a real control idea instead of just optimizing another prediction stack. If the details survive scrutiny, it could become useful conceptual scaffolding for future closed-loop epilepsy hardware.
notes.overview: The paper proposes passive neuromodulation, a closed-loop mechanism that uses analog feedback to drain energy from epileptic circuits rather than actively driving the tissue with conventional stimulation pulses. The authors test the idea in two very different seizure models: a detailed biophysical dentate-gyrus network model and the Epileptor neural mass model. They report seizure suppression in both settings and also test a responsive version that activates only briefly after seizure detection. The paper’s value is that it makes the intervention logic explicit: if pathological dynamics are sustained by excess network energy, then damping may be a more natural control strategy than repeated forcing.
